summary: Hydralazine is a direct arteriolar vasodilator that lowers peripheral vascular resistance to treat hypertension and, with isosorbide dinitrate, heart failure. Oral therapy starts at 10 mg four times daily and is titrated upward. It causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention (often offset by a beta-blocker and diuretic), and a dose- and duration-related drug-induced lupus-like syndrome, especially in slow acetylators. Other risks include angina precipitation and peripheral neuritis.
indications: Essential hypertension, alone or as an adjunct
Severe hypertension when oral therapy is not feasible or in hypertensive emergencies (parenteral)
Heart failure (adjunct, typically combined with isosorbide dinitrate, notably in self-identified Black patients)

dosage.d: 10 mg four times daily for 2-4 days, then 25 mg QID for the rest of week 1, then 50 mg QID
dosage.n: Maintain at lowest effective dose; max usually 300 mg/day

dosage.d: 10-20 mg IV or 10-50 mg IM, repeated as needed
dosage.n: Monitor BP closely; switch to oral when feasible

dosage.d: 0.75 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses; titrate over 3-4 weeks (max 7.5 mg/kg/day or 200 mg/day)
Titrate hydralazine up to ~75 mg three times daily as tolerated
dosage.n: Used as fixed-dose combination or separately

dosage.d: Use lower doses or longer dosing intervals
dosage.n: Higher plasma levels; greater lupus risk in slow acetylators

admin: Take oral doses consistently in relation to meals for reproducible absorption
Titrate gradually to limit reflex tachycardia and headache
Often combined with a beta-blocker (limits tachycardia) and a diuretic (limits fluid retention)
For parenteral use, monitor blood pressure frequently and use the lowest effective dose
Do not stop abruptly; taper to avoid rebound hypertension
moa: Hydralazine directly relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle (with little venous effect), reducing systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure. The vasodilation triggers a baroreceptor-mediated reflex increase in heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output, and activates the renin-angiotensin system causing sodium and fluid retention.

absolute: Coronary artery disease (risk of myocardial ischemia)
monitor: ANA titer and CBC for drug-induced lupus

preg: Hydralazine has long been used in pregnancy, including intravenously for severe hypertension and pre-eclampsia, and is generally considered acceptable when needed. Monitor for maternal hypotension and fetal effects; neonatal thrombocytopenia has been reported rarely.
lact: Hydralazine is excreted into breast milk in small amounts and is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; observe the infant for any unusual signs.
renal: In significant renal impairment, hydralazine is eliminated more slowly; reduce the dose or lengthen the dosing interval and titrate to response.
hepatic: Hepatic impairment reduces first-pass acetylation and increases plasma concentrations; use with caution and consider lower doses.

major: Other antihypertensives / diuretics - additive, possibly excessive, blood pressure lowering
MAO inhibitors - use with caution, marked hypotension
moderate: Beta-blockers - beneficial (limit reflex tachycardia) but additive hypotension; beta-blockers also raise hydralazine levels
minor: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) - may be needed to offset hydralazine-related neuropathy
interactions.food: Take consistently with food; food can affect bioavailability so keep timing uniform.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may potentiate hypotension; advise moderation.
interactions.diagnostics: Can induce positive ANA/anti-histone antibodies (drug-induced lupus); may cause positive Coombs test and reduced hemoglobin/blood counts.

serious: Drug-induced lupus-like syndrome (arthralgia, fever, rash, serositis)

monitoring: Blood pressure and heart rate regularly
CBC and ANA before and periodically during prolonged therapy
Symptoms of lupus-like syndrome (joint pain, fever, rash)
Signs of angina or ischemia, especially in CAD risk patients
Peripheral neuropathy; consider pyridoxine if it occurs
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed and keep meal timing consistent
Headache, flushing and a fast heartbeat are common early on and usually ease
Report joint pain, prolonged fever, rash or chest pain - these may signal a lupus-like reaction or heart strain
Do not stop suddenly; rise slowly to avoid dizziness
Tell your doctor about numbness or tingling in hands/feet
pk: Store tablets at 20-25 C; protect from light/moisture
pearls: Causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention - usually paired with a beta-blocker and a diuretic
Drug-induced lupus-like syndrome is dose/duration dependent and commoner in slow acetylators; usually reversible on stopping
Avoid in coronary artery disease - can precipitate angina/ischemia
Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) can treat or prevent hydralazine-induced peripheral neuropathy
Hydralazine-isosorbide dinitrate improves outcomes in heart failure, especially in self-identified Black patients
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and continue the regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Overdose causes hypotension, marked tachycardia, headache, flushing, myocardial ischemia and possible arrhythmias and shock. Management is supportive: place supine, give IV fluids for hypotension, and treat shock; avoid pure alpha-agonists that worsen ischemia. Beta-blockade can control severe tachycardia. Monitor cardiac status.
